result:
When the city took down the clock at Mercer and Ninth, they left its shadow on the wall: a pale circle above the pharmacy, with four little squares where the brackets had been. For thirty years I had looked up at that clock on my way to work. The morning it was gone, I looked at the circle and thought, quite distinctly, *I have plenty of time.*

I was late, of course.

The clock had always run seven minutes fast. This was useful to people who didn’t know it and useless to people who did. My father, who repaired watches in a shop across the street, considered it a personal insult. Once a week he wrote down the discrepancy on a postcard and mailed it to the Department of Public Works. After he died, I found a bundle of replies in his desk. The first twelve were form letters. The thirteenth said, in blue ink, “Dear Mr. Vale, I walk past it too. I know. Yours, Denise.”

There were no more postcards after that. Instead, there were Christmas cards from Denise.

I inherited the shop. Not the skill, unfortunately, just the lease and many shallow drawers full of screws small enough to inhale. I tried keeping it open. People came in with stopped watches, and I changed their batteries. If that didn’t work, I gave them directions to a man in Queens. Gradually the watch business became a key-cutting business, because the machine came with instructions and the instructions were good. My father’s name stayed on the window: VALE, HOROLOGIST. Below it I taped a sheet of paper that said KEYS $4.

The afternoon the clock disappeared, a woman came in carrying its minute hand.

It was nearly as long as her arm, black on one side and a startling clean white on the other.

“Denise?” I said.

“His daughter?” she said.

We shook hands across the counter. She had retired from Public Works years ago, but a friend on the crew had called her when they took the clock down. The housing was cracked. The motor had burned out. She had asked for the hand and, having obtained it, discovered she did not particularly want a large piece of municipal property in her apartment.

“I thought your father might like it,” she said, and then shut her eyes. “Listen to me. I went to his funeral.”

“He’d have hated it,” I said.

“Yes,” she said happily. “He would.”

We tried it in several places. Horizontal above the door, it looked like a direction nobody should follow. Upright beside the register, it looked like a sword. Finally Denise laid it on the floor to free her hands while she put her scarf back on. A customer stepped over it, collected two brass keys, stepped over it again, then came back from the sidewalk.

“Is that the minute hand?” he asked.

Soon there were six people in the shop. One remembered the clock being slow, not fast. Another insisted it had once had a second hand. A delivery driver said he’d spent a whole summer eating lunch beneath it and had never noticed it at all. Denise sat on the stool behind the counter and listened with the serene expression of a woman to whom none of these complaints could any longer be officially addressed.

At closing time, she bought a key.

“What for?” I asked.

“My front door.”

“I mean, do you need one?”

“Eventually,” she said.

After she left, I swept the floor. I turned off the lights. In the window, my father’s gold letters floated backward over the dark street. Across the way, the pale circle was still visible above the pharmacy. They would paint it soon, I thought, or the weather would darken it until nobody could find the edge.

I picked up the minute hand. At its base was a square hole, and the hole, by a coincidence my father could have expressed to three decimal places, fitted over the square spindle of the old awning crank.

I slid it on. It held.

In the morning I stood outside the shop and turned the minute hand. High above me, the striped canvas unrolled for the first time in years. Dust fell. Two dry leaves and a green plastic dinosaur dropped onto the pavement. The awning was faded almost to pink, except for the last foot, which had been rolled tight against the wall and was still a magnificent red.

At nine, Denise came by on her way to buy bread. She stood under the awning and looked up at the red stripe.

“Was that always there?”

“The color was.”

She considered this. Then she took the dinosaur, which she said her grandson would like, and went on down the street.

It rained that afternoon. People stopped beneath the awning to close umbrellas, open umbrellas, search for bus fare, finish phone calls. A boy waited there for his mother. A woman put down her groceries and divided the weight more evenly between two bags. Nobody came in for a key until nearly five.

I had the door propped open. I could hear the rain hitting the canvas, a good sound, surprisingly loud. When the woman with the groceries had finished rearranging them, she stayed another minute with her hands empty. I stayed where I was. Neither of us looked up.
